summary:
A Raconteur finance feature arguing that women-led deep-tech startups in Europe represent an overlooked, undervalued investment opportunity. It cites research that women-founded startups generate 78 cents of revenue per dollar invested versus 31 cents for male-founded ventures, yet all-female founding teams receive only 1.2% to 2.3% of European VC. In deep tech specifically, women are 14% of founders but attract 11.4% of investment, rising to 15% at seed. European Patent Office data show women appear on just 13.5% of European startup patent applications, and historically smaller rounds have led to lower valuations.

Alena Redeker, principal at Auxxo, argues the gap is structural rather than a conscious choice by investors, and that at pre-seed and seed the relevant question is upside potential rather than failure risk, since deep tech carries binary, moonshot outcomes.

The EU's Women TechEU programme, with a 12m euro budget, will award 75,000 euro equity-free grants to 160 early-stage women-led deep-tech startups, with 40% of funding reserved for "widening countries". Consortium representatives (Virginia Gomez of Sploro, Angele Giuliano and Rebecca Zammit of AcrossLimits) note grants rarely cover heavy deep-tech costs such as CE-marking and regulatory milestones, and that widening innovators lack access rather than talent.

Examples include PrintyMed (Latvia, founder Jekaterina Romanova), producing non-toxic artificial spider silk for bioengineered heart valves and implants, and MoveTru (Northern Ireland, founder Naomi McGregor), combining wearables and AI for women's sports medicine, which raised $1.9m pre-seed.

Prior Women TechEU cohorts converted 9m euros of public investment into 53.8m euros of private follow-on funding within a year. AwakenHub is expanding investor networks. Redeker concludes that increasing the share of women managing AUM is what genuinely reshifts capital toward female founders.

No relevance to workplace technology themes.
